title: Single-shot magic state factories for quantum LDPC codes
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can substantially reduce the qubit overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but any useful architecture based on such codes also requires an efficient mechanism to implement non-Clifford gates in a fault-tolerant manner. We introduce a space-time-efficient magic state factory for high-rate qLDPC codes by combining the transversal non-Clifford gates of recently developed tricycle codes with single-shot four-dimensional balanced product quadcycle codes. The key ingredient is an efficient "escape" mechanism that teleports postselected logical magic states from tricycle codes to larger distance quadcycle codes. Under a standard circuit-level noise model at physical error rate $10^{-3}$, our factories produce $\mathrm{CCZ}$ states at logical error rates as low as $10^{-9}$ with 10-40 times lower space-time cost than state-of-the-art magic state generation methods. The resulting states are directly encoded in high-rate blocks suitable for computation. We identify the quadcycle codes by an AI-assisted search and show that they can serve as excellent memories capable of single-shot error correction. Finally, we present a concrete implementation of the entire factory with highly efficient atom transport on reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computers. Together, these results provide an end-to-end, practical protocol for producing and utilizing high-fidelity magic states within a high-rate qLDPC architecture, with the lowest space-time cost to date.
summary:
**TL;DR** The authors build a magic-state factory that generates non-Clifford resource states transversally in 3D balanced-product "tricycle" codes and then teleports them, via a depth-1 homomorphic CNOT, into algebraically matched 4D "quadcycle" codes that have larger, balanced distances and are single-shot in both Pauli bases. At circuit-level depolarizing noise $p=10^{-3}$, the resulting CCZ states reach logical error rates of $1.2\times10^{-5}$ to $\sim10^{-8}$ at 10–40× lower expected space-time volume than surface- or color-code cultivation, and they arrive already encoded in a high-rate LDPC block.

**The big picture** Low-density parity-check codes promise far fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than the surface code, but nobody had a cheap, native way to produce the non-Clifford resource states that universal computation requires inside such codes. This work pairs two code families with shared algebraic structure: one is good at producing magic cheaply but cannot hold it, the other is good at holding and processing it but cannot produce it. A single layer of physical gates moves the magic from the first to the second, with postselection applied in the brief window where errors are detectable but the state is still cheap to throw away. The result is the lowest reported space-time cost for magic state production to date, delivered directly in the kind of high-rate block a downstream algorithm would use.

**Key contributions**
- Quadcycle codes: four-element abelian group-algebra (balanced/lifted product) CSS codes with $6n_G$ qubits, metachecks in *both* bases, an $X$–$Z$ duality forcing $d_X=d_Z$, and depth-1 translation automorphisms; concrete pairs from $[[54,6,6]]$ to $[[420,6,25]]$.
- The "escape": the quadcycle complex is the mapping cone of multiplication by $d$ on the tricycle complex, yielding a canonical embedding and a depth-1 transversal homomorphic CNOT covering all $k_{3\mathrm{D}}$ logicals ($k_{4\mathrm{D}}=2k_{3\mathrm{D}}$ saturated).
- A fan-out gadget (distance-2 repetition concatenation, reusing $Z$-ancilla qubits) that compresses the CCZ circuit from depth 2 to depth 1, preserving circuit distance; measured error exponents $3.11\pm0.04$ and $3.91\pm0.07$ confirm full-detection doubling of effective distance.
- Downstream gadgets: homomorphic measurement extracting two disjoint CCZ states from the nine-qubit $\det$ hypergraph state, plus teleported CZ fix-ups.
- Explicit neutral-atom compilation: monomials act as uniform AOD row/column translations; constant number of array traversals per operation.

**How it works** Three tricycle blocks in $|\bar+\rangle$ receive a depth-1 transversal CCZ producing the $|\det_3\rangle$ hypergraph state; three quadcycle blocks are prepared single-shot in $|\bar0\rangle$; one transversal CNOT layer teleports the magic; transversal $X$ readout of the tricycle blocks supplies both Pauli-frame corrections and full detector-based postselection. Simulations are in Stim under SD6 with a three-qubit depolarizing CCZ channel ($p_{\mathrm{CCZ}}=p,2p$), decoded by most-likely-error; quadcycle memory uses sliding-window ($W=3,S=1$) single-shot decoding.

**Why it matters** This closes the main missing piece of qLDPC architectures — a native, high-throughput non-Clifford source that preserves the rate advantage — and should interest anyone doing fault-tolerant resource estimation or neutral-atom architecture design.

**Caveats** Only a single tricycle–quadcycle pair is simulated; cross-block CCZ correlations are traced out, and full-factory yield is the cube of the quoted per-block acceptance. Space-time accounting excludes the homomorphic logical measurements, CZ fix-ups, injection surgery, and decoder latency (also excluded for the baselines). Larger-code distances come from Stern's algorithm, and the $[[162,6,14]]$ point at $p=10^{-3}$ is extrapolated as $p^{d/2}$ with $d=12$. Soundness is established only for some codes, and MLE decoding is not real-time-practical.

title: Error-Corrected Memory and Logic on a Heavy-Hex Superconducting-Qubit Processor
abstract: Large quantum computations require high-fidelity error-corrected memory and fault-tolerant logical operations. To achieve these with superconducting circuits, quantum processors will need many components operating with low error rates. In practice, fabrication of monolithic superconducting devices produces unavoidable heterogeneity in component performance, which the quantum computer must accommodate. We implement strategies to operate a large dynamic compass code on an array of 156 superconducting qubits arranged on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, making use of the entire monolithic quantum processor and redesigning our measurement schedule to exclude underperforming components. We demonstrate improvements of up to $35\%$ in logical error probabilities for a memory experiment by using a noise-informed decoder combined with strategies to exclude the worst-performing qubits and couplers, along with post-selecting on shots with a low probability of leakage errors. In addition to these memory results, we also observe performance gains of up to $56\%$ when these strategies are applied to measurement-based logic, demonstrated by stability experiments. We furthermore demonstrate high-fidelity fault-tolerant logic through lattice surgery. Through pre-selection filtering techniques, we can obtain Bell fidelities above $77\%$, and further logical gap post-selection using exclusive decoding increases these fidelities to above $97\%$. Our experiments demonstrate that high performance can be maintained in key elements of fault-tolerant quantum memory and logic when working on monolithic superconducting quantum processors with underperforming components, by using a suite of noise-informed quantum error correction strategies.
summary:
**TL;DR** The authors run a distance-scaled dynamic compass (Floquet-like) code across all 156 qubits of an IBM Heron heavy-hex chip, combining ACES-derived circuit-level Pauli noise models, explicit exclusion of two bad qubits and their couplers, and IQ-based leakage post-selection to cut logical error per round by ~32–35% in memory (to 4.11% in Z, 2.56% in X) and failure probability by up to 56% in 30-round stability experiments. Lattice surgery between two small patches reaches Bell fidelity lower bounds of 77.3% with pre-selection alone and >97% with logical-gap post-selection at 27% relative yield.

**The big picture** Real superconducting chips are not uniform: a handful of qubits or couplers are often one to two orders of magnitude noisier than the median, and these outliers can dominate the error rate of any code large enough to cover them. This work shows that simply refusing to use the bad components — redesigning the sequence of parity checks so the code routes around them — plus feeding the decoder a carefully measured, device-specific noise model and discarding runs where atoms of the processor have leaked out of their computational states, recovers most of the lost performance across memory, logical measurement, and a two-patch merge-and-split logic operation. It is a practical demonstration that monolithic, imperfect processors can still be pushed toward the regime where bigger codes help rather than hurt.

**Key contributions**
- First defect-exclusion construction for the dynamic compass code on a heavy-hex array: gauge checks are deformed into superstabilizers avoiding dead qubits (weight-2/3 X checks, weight-1 Z checks; stabilizer weight grows from 8 to at most 10 near defects).
- Full-device 7×7 memory on 156 qubits, reaching parity with the *median* 5×5 patch in Z and beating the mean 5×5 patch in X once defects are excluded.
- Demonstration that defect exclusion yields a roughly constant ~27–28% gain even with an ACES-informed BeliefMatching decoder — decoders cannot absorb defects.
- Stability experiments with 16 checks/round showing continued error suppression out to 30 rounds only with defect exclusion (plateau at ~12 rounds otherwise), attributed to leakage, not Pauli noise.
- Leakage/code-space *pre*-selection for lattice surgery (abort before running), plus exclusive-decoder logical-gap and belief-propagation-convergence post-selection.

**How it works** ACES supplies layer-specific Pauli error rates as BeliefMatching priors; IQ readout data is fit to Gaussian mixtures over |0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩ to give per-shot leakage probabilities (cut at 0.9 memory / 0.7 stability) and soft measurement-error priors. Bell fidelity is bounded from ⟨X̄X̄⟩ and ⟨Z̄Z̄⟩ since ⟨ȲȲ⟩ is inaccessible.

**Why it matters** Relevant to anyone building or decoding on monolithic superconducting hardware: it quantifies the relative payoff of better noise models versus hardware-aware code surgery, and shows leakage is the dominant ceiling on long logical operations.

**Caveats** Everything is above threshold — 3×3 patches still beat 7×7. Lattice surgery uses only d=3-scale patches and leans heavily on selection (total yield 4.55% for the best 3×3 result; pre-selection alone discards 86.7% of attempts). No mid-circuit reset halves timelike distance. Some ACES models came from different days or slightly different circuits. Only BeliefMatching was tested; stronger decoders might change the defect-exclusion conclusion. The soft-information/ACES redundancy is observed in stability only, with unclear generality.

title: On PPT entanglement distillation
abstract: We study entanglement distillation under operations that remain completely positive under partial-transpose conjugation, a.k.a. PPT channels, in the standard quantum Shannon theory regime of asymptotically vanishing but non-zero error. Our main results are: (a) a regularised formula for the PPT distillable entanglement in terms of a measured-relative-entropy-like quantity; and (b) two different single-letter converses, one based on operator quadratic forms and the other on Hirschman's strengthening of the Hadamard three-line theorem. As an immediate application of (b), we show that the PPT distillable entanglement can be strictly smaller than the regularised Rains bound, thereby resolving an open problem in the theory of entanglement manipulation [Regula et al., NJP 21:103017, 2019]. A gap appears already for $3\times 3$ Werner states: at antisymmetric weight $25/26$, a certified upper bound of $0.62107$ ebits lies below the (regularised) Rains bound, which equals $\frac{25}{26} \log_2 5 - \log_2 3 \approx 0.64766$ ebits. On a different note, (a) implies a faithful lower bound on the PPT distillable entanglement in terms of the entanglement negativity, which provides a quantitative counterpart to the qualitatively known fact that any NPT state is PPT distillable [Eggeling et al., PRL 87:257902, 2001].

\title{On PPT entanglement distillation}

\author{Ludovico Lami}
\email{ludovico.lami@gmail.com}
\affiliation{Scuola Normale Superiore, Piazza dei Cavalieri 7, 56126 Pisa, Italy}

\begin{abstract}
We study entanglement distillation under operations that remain completely positive under partial-transpose conjugation, a.k.a.\ PPT channels, in the standard quantum Shannon theory regime of asymptotically vanishing but non-zero error. Our main results are: (a)~a regularised formula for the PPT distillable entanglement in terms of a measured-relative-entropy-like quantity; and (b)~two different single-letter converses, one based on operator quadratic forms and the other on Hirschman's strengthening of the Hadamard three-line theorem. As an immediate application of~(b), we show that the PPT distillable entanglement can be strictly smaller than the regularised Rains bound, thereby resolving an open problem in the theory of entanglement manipulation~\href{https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1367-2630/ab4732}{[Regula et al., \emph{NJP} 21:103017, 2019]}. A gap appears already for $3\times 3$ Werner states: at antisymmetric weight $25/26$, a certified upper bound of $0.62107$ ebits lies below the (regularised) Rains bound, which equals $\frac{25}{26} \log_2 5 - \log_2 3 \approx 0.64766$ ebits. On a different note, (a)~implies a faithful lower bound on the PPT distillable entanglement in terms of the entanglement negativity, which provides a quantitative counterpart to the qualitatively known fact that any NPT state is PPT distillable~\href{https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.257902}{[Eggeling et al., \emph{PRL} 87:257902, 2001]}.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\noindent \textbf{Note.} The main results and techniques presented here have been derived almost entirely by ChatGPT Astra. The human author (yours truly) gave many suggestions on how to extend and generalise the initial findings, which applied only to Werner states, and spent many hours (but an order of magnitude fewer than would have been needed a year ago) validating and improving the proof techniques, as well as adapting the presentation to his style.

\subsection{Background}

Understanding asymptotic entanglement manipulation is a truly daring endeavour. For how central the phenomenon is for foundations~\cite{Werner, Aspect, dense-coding, teleportation, Ekert91} as well as applications~\cite{teleportation-experiment, entanglement-1200-km, entanglement-optical-clock, DIQKD-experiment, distributed-quantum-computing}, we only have a limited knowledge of the ultimate operational constraints on entanglement transformation in the asymptotic regime, where arbitrarily many copies of a given source state are available.
A particularly challenging task, in this sense, is entanglement distillation~\cite{Bennett-distillation, Bennett-distillation-mixed, Bennett-error-correction, devetak2005}, which consists in turning copies of a noisy, possibly mixed quantum state into as many `ebits' as possible with asymptotically vanishing error. Here, an ebit, also called two-qubit maximally entangled state or Bell pair, can be thought of as the `golden unit' of entanglement, since it is the fuel on which many quantum information processing protocols run. The ultimate rate of ebit production that is achievable from copies of a state $\rho = \rho_{AB}$ through local operations and classical communication (LOCC) is called the LOCC distillable entanglement of $\rho$, and denoted $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho)$. 

Calculating $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho)$ for even very simple mixed states $\rho$ is typically an extremely challenging task. As far as the author is aware, it is even unclear whether $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho)$ is Turing computable at all. Roughly speaking, the nature of this difficulty can be traced back to three different obstacles:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item The set of LOCC operations is mathematically complicated to describe and analyse~\cite{LOCC}.
\item The presence of the approximation error makes the output of the distillation protocol a moving target.
\item The asymptotic limit of an arbitrarily high number of input copies is analytically intractable, as we have no guarantee on how many copies may be needed to enable distillation~\cite{Watrous2004}.
\end{enumerate}
A possible approach to the problem is to separate these three obstacles, tackling them first one by one, and then in pairs, with the goal of eventually being able to tackle all three at once. 

\subsection{Prior work}

A popular idea to remove obstacle~(1) without trivialising the problem is that of replacing LOCC operations with quantum channels that completely preserve the property of having a non-negative partial transpose~\cite{PeresPPT}, also called PPT channels~\cite{Rains1999, Rains2001}. When acting on a bipartite system $A:B$ and outputting a (possibly different) bipartite system $A':B'$, PPT channels can also be defined as those whose Choi state~\cite{Choi} is PPT across the bipartition $AA':BB'$. Therefore, importantly, PPT-ness is a positive semi-definite constraint, entailing that it can be treated efficiently within the formalism of semi-definite programs (SDPs)~\cite{BOYD, vandenberghe_1996}. PPT channels form a (strict) superset of LOCC, meaning that the PPT distillable entanglement of a state is no smaller than its LOCC counterpart: formally, 
\bb
E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho) \leq E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho)\, .
\ee
Hence, any upper bound on $E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho)$ automatically yields an upper bound on $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho)$. It is in this way that one of the most powerful upper bounds on $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho)$, called the \emph{Rains bound}, was derived~\cite{Rains2001}. This is defined as
\bb
R(\rho) \coloneqq \inf_{\sigma \geq 0\,:\ \|\sigma^{\pt}\|_1\leq 1} D(\rho\|\sigma)\, ;
\ee
here, $D(\rho\|\sigma) \coloneqq \Tr \rho(\log \rho - \log \sigma)$ is the Umegaki relative entropy~\cite{Umegaki1962}, $\Gamma$ denotes the partial transpose on $B$, identified with the linear map satisfying $(X\otimes Y)^{\pt} = X \otimes Y^\intercal$, and $\|Z\|_1\coloneqq \Tr \sqrt{Z^\dag Z}$ denotes the trace norm. Note that the optimisation variable $\sigma$ does not need to be a state\,---\,it can be merely \emph{sub}-normalised, meaning that $\Tr \sigma\leq 1$.\footnote{Sub-normalisation is needed because $1\geq \left\|\sigma^{\pt}\right\|_1 \geq \Tr \sigma^{\pt} = \Tr \sigma$.} The tightest known bound on $E_{d,\,\ppt}$, and one of the tightest known on $E_{d,\,\locc}$, is obtained by \emph{regularising} the Rains bound, i.e.\ by computing its asymptotic value in the limit of arbitrarily many copies:
\bb
E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho) \leq E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho) \leq R^\infty(\rho) \coloneqq \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n\, R\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, .
\label{Rains_bound}
\ee
For context, the \emph{only} other (upper) bound on $E_{d,\,\locc}$ that, to the best of our knowledge, can sometimes compete with the regularised Rains bound in~\eqref{Rains_bound} is the \emph{squashed entanglement}~\cite{Tucci1999, squashed, rel-ent-sq, Shirokov-sq}. It is known that, in general, the regularisation in~\eqref{Rains_bound} is necessary~\cite{nonadditivity-Rains}. However, unlike many other regularised measures in quantum information theory, $R^\infty$ can actually be shown to be computable, with precise runtime guarantees~\cite{FFF2025}.

Throughout this paper, we will deal with PPT operations instead of the much more complex set of LOCC operations, thereby softening the above obstacle~(1). The key question we face in this work is:
\begin{center}

\it At least for PPT instead of LOCC operations, can we tackle obstacles~(2) and~(3) together?

\end{center}
It is worth remarking that, \emph{if we accept removing also obstacle~(2)}, namely, if we look at exact, zero-error transformations, then much more is known. The task of dilution rather than distillation, in the PPT zero-error case, has been solved completely, first in~\cite{Martin-exact-PPT} for states with vanishing bi-negativity\,---\,in particular, for all two-qubit states~\cite{Ishizaka2004}\,---\,and then in~\cite{PPT-zerocost} for general states. This latter paper built on a previous claimed solution to the problem~\cite{Xin-exact-PPT, Wang2023}, which however turned out to have a serious issue~\cite{Xin-Mark-errata}. See also the recent work~\cite{Brinster2026}. As for distillation, the optimal PPT rate that is achievable with zero error was conjectured to reduce to the min-Rains relative entropy~\cite{Wang2016, nonadditivity-Rains}, a statement that was disproved very recently~\cite{Zhu2026}.

Here, we will leave aside these results, which deal with a setting in which both obstacles~(1) and~(2) have been artificially tamed, and focus on the setting in which only~(1) has been removed artificially (by relaxing LOCC to PPT) but~(2) and~(3) are dealt with together. We will therefore look at the theory of PPT entanglement manipulation in the asymptotically vanishing error setting. In this setting, much less is known from the prior literature. Here is a summary of what we do know:
\begin{itemize}
\item The theory of PPT entanglement manipulation is asymptotically irreversible~\cite{irreversibility-PPT}, something that cannot be amended even by going to the wider class of PPT-preserving operations~\cite{irreversibility}; however, we currently have no expressions for either the PPT distillable entanglement or the PPT entanglement cost.

\item We suspect that the first inequality in~\eqref{Rains_bound} is not tight in general, as \emph{NPT bound entangled states}, i.e.\ states that are not PPT but such that $E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho) = 0$, are conjectured to exist~\cite{HorodeckiBound, Horodecki-open-problems}. Any such state would necessarily satisfy $E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho) > 0$, because every NPT state is distillable with PPT operations~\cite{Eggeling2001}:
\bb
\rho^\Gamma \not\geq 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho) > 0\, .
\label{NPT_states_are_PPT_distillable}
\ee
A remarkable feature of the above result is that it is exquisitely qualitative, in that no lower bound on $E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho)$ is stated based on the \emph{entanglement negativity}~\cite{negativity} of $\rho$.

\item What about the second inequality in~\eqref{Rains_bound}? 

In~\cite[Section~3.1.1]{Regula2019}, it is explicitly conjectured that it be an equality for all states:
\bb
E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho) \eqt{?} R^\infty(\rho)\, .
\label{Bartosz_conjecture}
\ee
Solving this conjecture, or otherwise finding an alternative formula for $E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho)$, would mark a decisive step forward in our understanding of PPT operations.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Our contributions}

In this paper, we investigate in a systematic way entanglement distillation under PPT operations in the regime of asymptotically vanishing error. Our main results are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]

\item In Theorem~\ref{regularised_formula_thm}, we establish a regularised formula for the PPT distillable entanglement $E_{d,\,\ppt}$. This formula can be used to calculate achievable rates (i.e.\ lower bounds on $E_{d,\,\ppt}$) systematically, but we have not yet been able to provide any guarantees on the speed of convergence. As a byproduct, it yields an explicit faithful lower bound in terms of the entanglement negativity: writing $N(\rho)\coloneqq(\|\rho^\Gamma\|_1-1)/2$ and $d\coloneqq\min\{d_A,d_B\}$, we obtain $E_{d,\,\ppt}(\rho)\geq1-h_2\!\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac{N(\rho)}{d+1}\right)$. This makes the qualitative asymptotic statement~\eqref{NPT_states_are_PPT_distillable} quantitative by supplying a strictly positive rate whenever $N(\rho)>0$.

\item Then, in Theorems~\ref{quadratic_converse_thm} and~\ref{analytic_converse_thm} we prove two different converse bounds, i.e.\ two upper bounds on $E_{d,\,\ppt}$ that are valid for any state. These are quite different in nature: the one in Theorem~\ref{quadratic_converse_thm} is based on quadratic forms, while that in Theorem~\ref{analytic_converse_thm} is based on the theory of analytic functions.

Since every LOCC operation is PPT, these converses also upgrade the best available (computable) upper bounds on the LOCC distillable entanglement to
\bb
E_{d,\,\locc}(\rho) \leq \min\big\{ R^\infty(\rho),\, E_{\mathrm{sq}}(\rho),\, E_Q(\rho),\, E_A(\rho)\big\}\, .
\label{LOCC_converse_bounds}
\ee
Here, $E_{\mathrm{sq}}$ denotes the squashed entanglement~\cite{Tucci1999, squashed, rel-ent-sq, Shirokov-sq}. The last two bounds are new, and are defined in~\eqref{quadratic_bound} and~\eqref{analytic_bound}, respectively.

\item A remarkable consequence of our converses is that the conjectured equality~\eqref{Bartosz_conjecture} between the PPT distillable entanglement and the regularised Rains bound is, alas, false: in Theorem~\ref{gap_Werner_thm}, we find that, already for a $3\times 3$ Werner state with antisymmetric weight $25/26$, we have $\Eppt(\rho_{25/26}) \leq 0.62107 < \frac{25}{26}\log5 - \log3 = R^\infty(\rho_{25/26})$.

\end{enumerate}

\section{Main results}
\label{main_results_sec}

All systems are finite dimensional and logarithms are base two. We write $\Gamma$ for the partial transpose on the second party in a fixed product basis. A state is PPT if $\rho^{\pt} \geq 0$, and a channel $\Lambda$ is PPT if $\Gamma_{\rm out}\circ\Lambda\circ\Gamma_{\rm in}$ is completely positive. The PPT distillable entanglement $\Eppt(\rho)$ is the asymptotic number of ebits per copy obtainable with vanishing error. We also consider its strong-converse threshold $\Eppt^\dag(\rho)$, above which the optimal overlap with the target maximally entangled state tends to zero, and the lower exponential decay rate $\EpptErr(\rho,R)$ of that overlap at rate $R$. Precise operational definitions are given in Section~\ref{setting_sec}.

For $\Phi_d = \frac1d \sum_{i,j = 1}^d \ketbraa{ii}{jj}$, the normalised maximally entangled state, write
\bb
F_{\PPT}(\rho,d) \coloneqq \sup_{\Lambda\in\PPT}\Tr\big[\Phi_d\Lambda(\rho)\big]\, ,
\label{bell_overlap_definition}
\ee
where the supremum is over PPT channels with the indicated output spaces. At rate $R \geq 0$, the exponent is
\bb
\EpptErr(\rho,R) \coloneqq \liminf_{n\to\infty} - \frac1n\log F_{\PPT}\!\left(\rho^{\otimes n},\left\lceil 2^{nR}\right\rceil\right), \qquad R \geq 0\, .
\label{distillation_error_exponent}
\ee
A positive exponent gives an exponential strong converse.

\subsection{A regularised formula}

Our first result expresses the distillation rate through a measurement optimisation. Let $\MM$ be a finite measurement channel represented by the POVM $(E_j)_j$, and define
\bb
L(\rho) \coloneqq \sup_{\MM}\sum_{j:\ \Tr[\rho E_j]>0}\Tr[\rho E_j]\log\frac{\Tr[\rho E_j]}{\big\|E_j^{\pt}\big\|_\infty}\, ,\qquad L^\infty(\rho) \coloneqq \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n L\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, .
\label{L_definition}
\ee
Zero effects are omitted. The limit exists by superadditivity and the logarithmic-negativity upper bound proved in Proposition~\ref{FG_properties_prop}. Unlike a finite-error operational optimisation, $L$ contains neither an output dimension nor a fidelity constraint.

Rains's projective-measurement bound~\cite[Theorem~6.4]{Rains2001} is recovered by restricting the POVM to orthogonal projections. Allowing arbitrary POVMs and then regularising gives an equality with the operational rate. The converse direction uses the two-outcome measurement obtained by pulling back the Bell test of a distillation protocol; the direct direction combines a fixed measurement with classical typicality. Thus the same explicit functional accounts for both sides of the rate formula.

\begin{thm}[(Regularised formula for the PPT distillable entanglement)] \label{regularised_formula_thm}
For every finite-dimensional bipartite state, with $L$ defined by~\eqref{L_definition},
\bb
\Eppt(\rho) = L^\infty(\rho) = \sup_{n\in\N^+}\frac1n\,L\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, .
\label{regularisation}
\ee
\end{thm}

For a state with computable entries, Theorem~\ref{regularised_formula_thm} gives a computable increasing sequence of lower bounds converging to $\Eppt(\rho)$: finite rational POVMs and positive rational weights can be enumerated, and the corresponding scores can be approximated from below. Thus $\Eppt$ is lower semicomputable. This also follows directly by searching over finite-block PPT channels and applying the hashing inequality to their outputs~\cite{devetak2005}; no new computability status is claimed here. Had $\Eppt$ equalled $R^\infty$, the algorithms of~\cite{FFF2025} would have established its Turing computability. Our separation rules out that identification, but does not rule out computability by another method; the existence of a convergent computable family of upper bounds remains open.

For the proofs and sharper finite-block lower bounds, we retain an auxiliary quantity $\widetilde{L}$, defined in~\eqref{povm_regularised_scores}, whose regularisation $\widetilde{L}^{\,\infty}$ also equals $\Eppt$. It keeps the operator absolute values before taking a norm. This additional structure gives simple spectral lower bounds and the one-copy Werner calculation, but is unnecessary in the statement of Theorem~\ref{regularised_formula_thm}.

\subsection{Two converse constructions}

Our two upper bounds use different information about a distillation test. The first controls a quadratic form on the test, including correlations with an ancillary system. The second places the input in an analytic family and combines bounds on both boundary circles of an annulus. Both retain enough finite-block information to prove exponential strong converses, beyond an upper bound on vanishing-error rates.

For the quadratic construction, the operator space carries the Hilbert--Schmidt scalar product $\Braket{X,Y} = \Tr[X^\dag Y]$. Write $\LL_\omega(X) \coloneqq \omega X$. For $\alpha>0$ and a strictly positive super-operator $\KK$ on this space, define
\bb
V_\alpha[\omega,\KK] \coloneqq \frac1\alpha\Braket{\sqrt\omega,\,\big(\log\big(\LL_{\sqrt\omega}\circ\KK^{-1}\circ\LL_{\sqrt\omega}\big)\big)(\sqrt\omega)}\, .
\label{V_definition}
\ee
Here $\omega \geq 0$ may be singular, and the logarithm is restricted to the support of the super-operator. The vector $\sqrt\omega$ lies in that support. Positivity of super-operators refers to the Hilbert--Schmidt scalar product, not to complete positivity.

\begin{thm}[(Conditional quadratic converse)]\label{quadratic_converse_thm}
Let $\rho = \rho_{A:B}$ be a bipartite state. With $V_\alpha$ defined by~\eqref{V_definition}, put
\bb
E_Q(\rho) = E_Q(\rho_{A:B}) \coloneqq \inf_{\rho_{AA':BB'},\,\alpha,\KK,\JJ} \left\{V_\alpha[\rho_{AA':BB'},\KK] - V_\alpha[\rho_{A':B'},\JJ]\right\} ,
\label{quadratic_bound}
\ee
where the infimum is over all finite-dimensional extensions $\rho_{AA':BB'}$ of $\rho_{A:B}$, all $\alpha>0$, and all strictly positive super-operators $\KK,\JJ$ on the operator spaces of $AA'BB'$ and $A'B'$, respectively, satisfying
\bb
\Braket{Q_n\otimes X_n,\KK^{\otimes n}[Q_n\otimes X_n]} \leq \big\|Q_n^{\Gamma_{B^n}}\big\|_\infty^\alpha\Braket{X_n,\JJ^{\otimes n}[X_n]}
\label{ancillary_form_all_copies}
\ee
for all $n\in\N^+$, all tests $0 \leq Q_n \leq \id$ on $A^nB^n$, and all operators $X_n$ on $(A'B')^n$. Then
\bb
\Eppt(\rho_{A:B}) \leq \Eppt^\dag(\rho_{A:B}) \leq E_Q(\rho_{A:B})\, .
\label{conditional}
\ee
Every rate strictly above $E_Q(\rho_{A:B})$ has an exponential strong converse. 

\end{thm}

The all-copy hypothesis is a substantive constraint; it cannot in general be replaced by its one-copy version. Geometric means of positive super-operators turn this quadratic control into data processing for $V_\alpha$. Conditioning on an ancillary system then subtracts the corresponding ancillary contribution. The choice of right multiplication recovers the Rains bound, while different quadratic forms can improve it, as the Werner example below shows.

For positive operators, we write
\bb
D(X\|Y) \coloneqq \Tr\big[X(\log X - \log Y)\big] \quad\text{if }\supp X \subseteq \supp Y\, ,
\label{relative_entropy_definition}
\ee
and set $D(X\|Y) = +\infty$ otherwise. Our relative entropy for a subnormalised second argument has no trace correction.

The sandwiched R\'enyi relative entropy~\cite{tomamichel12smooth_tutorial, Wilde2014, newRenyi} is
\bb
\widetilde D_\alpha(\rho\|\sigma) \coloneqq \frac1{\alpha - 1}\log\Tr\!\left[ \left(\sigma^{\frac{1 - \alpha}{2\alpha}}\rho \sigma^{\frac{1 - \alpha}{2\alpha}}\right)^\alpha\right], \qquad \alpha>1\, ,
\label{sandwiched_renyi}
\ee
when $\supp\rho\subseteq\supp\sigma$, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. Negative powers are restricted to $\supp\sigma$.

The analytic converse uses an explicit positive weight on the two boundary circles. For $0<\theta<1$, put
\bb
\beta_\theta(s) \coloneqq \frac{\sin(\pi\theta)}{2\theta\bigl(\cosh(\pi s) + \cos(\pi\theta)\bigr)},\qquad s\in\mathbb R\, .
\label{hirschman_density}
\ee
For an annulus $\mathcal{O} = \{z:a<|z-c|<b\}$ and an interior point $z_* = c + r e^{i\varphi}$, write $\ell \coloneqq \ln(b/a)$ and $\theta \coloneqq \ln(r/a)/\ell$. Define the boundary density
\bb
k_{\mathcal{O},z_*}\!\left(c + a e^{i\psi}\right) &\coloneqq \frac{1 - \theta}{a\ell}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\beta_{1 - \theta}\!\left(\frac{\psi - \varphi + 2\pi m}{\ell}\right),\\
k_{\mathcal{O},z_*}\!\left(c + b e^{i\psi}\right) &\coloneqq \frac{\theta}{b\ell}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\beta_\theta\!\left(\frac{\psi - \varphi + 2\pi m}{\ell}\right)\, .
\label{explicit_annular_density}
\ee
The series converge uniformly and define positive $2\pi$-periodic functions. With respect to positive arclength $|\mathrm dz|$, the inner and outer weights have masses $1 - \theta$ and $\theta$, respectively. Their sum is one, and no orientation of either circle is involved.

\begin{thm}[(Analytic-family strong converse)]\label{analytic_converse_thm}
Let $\rho = \rho_{A:B}$ be a finite-dimensional bipartite state, let $\mathcal{O} = \{z\in\mathbb C:a<|z - c|<b\}$ with $c\in\mathbb C$ and $0<a<b$, and let $Z(z)$ be an operator on $AB$, analytic in a neighbourhood of $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$, with $\Tr[Z(z)] = 1$. Suppose that $z_*\in\mathcal{O}$, $\sigma = Z(z_*)$ is a state, and $\supp\rho\subseteq\supp\sigma$. With the density in~\eqref{explicit_annular_density}, built from~\eqref{hirschman_density}, define
\bb
J_{Z,\mathcal{O},z_*}(R) \coloneqq \int_{\partial\mathcal{O}} \min\!\left\{\log\|Z(z)\|_1,\,\log\big\|Z(z)^{\pt_B}\big\|_1 - R\right\}k_{\mathcal{O},z_*}(z)\,|\mathrm dz|\, .
\label{analytic_J}
\ee
If $R \geq 0$ and $D(\rho\|\sigma) + J_{Z,\mathcal{O},z_*}(R)<0$, then $R$ is an exponential strong-converse rate for PPT distillation of $\rho$. Specifically,
\bb
\EpptErr(\rho,R) \geq \sup_{\alpha>1}\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha}\Big[ - J_{Z,\mathcal{O},z_*}(R) - \widetilde D_\alpha(\rho\|\sigma)\Big]>0\, .
\label{analytic_error_exponent}
\ee
\end{thm}

The analytic family need not consist of states away from the reference point. This freedom is useful: trace-norm duality supplies two different boundary bounds, and Hirschman's inequality averages their smaller value with positive weights. Quantum hypothesis testing then transfers the resulting exponential bound from the reference state to the input. For a fixed reference family this yields an explicit scalar boundary integral, while optimisation over families gives the converse $E_A$ defined in~\eqref{analytic_bound}.

\subsection{A strict gap from the regularised Rains bound}

For local dimension $d$, let $F_d$ be the swap, $P_0 = (\id + F_d)/2$ and $P_1 = (\id - F_d)/2$. The Werner states are
\bb
\rho_p \coloneqq (1 - p)\frac{2P_0}{d(d + 1)} + p\frac{2P_1}{d(d - 1)}\, ,\qquad 0 \leq p \leq 1\, ,\quad d \geq 2\, .
\label{werner}
\ee
The regularised Rains bound $R^\infty$, defined in~\eqref{rains_definition}, is a standard upper bound on $\Eppt$. It was not known whether this bound always gives the PPT distillation rate~\cite{Regula2019}. The following separation shows that it does not, already for qutrit Werner states.

Symmetry makes the relevant calculations small enough to certify. On the lower-bound side, Werner twirling converts collective POVMs into a finite linear program, and one feasible $48$-copy POVM certifies the displayed rate. For the converse, the symmetric and antisymmetric sectors reduce a quadratic-form comparison to two dimensions. \section{Setting and operational reduction}
\label{setting_sec}

We retain the conventions of Section~\ref{main_results_sec}. On $n$ copies, partial transpose acts on the entire second party of the bipartition $A^n:B^n$. Channels are completely positive and trace preserving, and $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm.

\subsection{One-shot and asymptotic quantities}

For $\e \in (0,1)$, define the one-shot PPT distillable entanglement by the hypothesis-testing expression
\bb
\Eppt^{(1),\,\e}(\rho) \coloneqq - \log \inf_{\substack{0 \leq Q \leq \id\\
\Tr \rho Q \geq 1 - \e}} \big\|Q^{\pt}\big\|_\infty\, .
\label{one_shot_ppt}
\ee
Rigorously speaking, the largest achievable integer Schmidt rank at error $\e$ is $\lfloor2^{\Eppt^{(1),\,\e}(\rho)}\rfloor$, by Rains's semidefinite program~\cite[Theorem~3.1]{Rains2001}. Taking its logarithm changes~\eqref{one_shot_ppt} by less than one bit, which is asymptotically irrelevant.

The PPT distillable entanglement and its strong-converse threshold are, respectively,
\bb
\Eppt(\rho) & \coloneqq \lim_{\e \to 0^+}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\Eppt^{(1),\,\e}(\rho^{\otimes n})\, ,\\
\Eppt^\dag(\rho) & \coloneqq \lim_{\e \to 1^-}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\Eppt^{(1),\,\e}(\rho^{\otimes n})\, .
\label{operational_rate}
\ee
Thus the first quantity describes rates achievable with vanishing error, whereas every rate above the second forces the best Bell overlap to tend to zero.

For an integer $d \geq 1$, the optimal Bell overlap in~\eqref{bell_overlap_definition} has the semidefinite representation
\bb
F_{\PPT}(\rho,d) = \max\left\{\Tr \rho Q:\ 0 \leq Q \leq \id,\ \big\|Q^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq d^{-1}\right\} .
\label{optimal_overlap}
\ee
The exponent in~\eqref{distillation_error_exponent} measures decay of this overlap, rather than of its square root.

For completeness, we recall the implementation of~\eqref{optimal_overlap}. A PPT channel gives $Q = \Lambda^\dag(\Phi_d)$ satisfying
\bb
0 \leq Q \leq \id,\qquad \big\|Q^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq d^{-1}\, ,
\label{effect}
\ee
because its conjugate adjoint is unital positive. Conversely, for $d \geq 2$, such a test defines the channel
\bb
\Lambda_Q(X) = \Tr[XQ]\Phi_d + \Tr\big[X(\id - Q)\big]\frac{\id - \Phi_d}{d^2 - 1}\, .
\label{channel}
\ee
Writing $P_\pm = (\id \pm F_d)/2$, where $F_d$ is the target swap, its transpose conjugate is
\bb
(\Gamma_{\rm out} \circ \Lambda_Q \circ \Gamma_{\rm in})(X) = \frac{\Tr\big[X(\id + dQ^{\pt})\big]}{d(d + 1)}P_+ + \frac{\Tr\big[X(\id - dQ^{\pt})\big]}{d(d - 1)}P_-\, .
\ee
Both coefficient matrices are positive, proving complete positivity. At $d = 1$ the optimal overlap is trivially one.

For binary probabilities we use $h_2(a) = - a\log a - (1 - a)\log(1 - a)$ and $\Dbin(a\|b) = a\log(a/b) + (1 - a)\log\big((1 - a)/(1 - b)\big)$, with the usual continuous endpoint conventions. 

\subsection{The Rains bound}
\label{rains_prelim_sec}

The Rains set, its relative entropy, and the corresponding regularisation are~\cite{Rains2001}
\bb
\mathcal{R}(A:B) & \coloneqq \left\{\sigma_{AB} \geq 0:\ \big\|\sigma_{AB}^{\pt_B}\big\|_1 \leq 1\right\} ,\\
R(\rho) & \coloneqq \inf_{\sigma\in\mathcal{R}(A:B)}D(\rho\|\sigma), \qquad R^\infty(\rho) \coloneqq \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n R(\rho^{\otimes n})\, .
\label{rains_definition}
\ee
Tensor closure of $\mathcal{R}$ makes $R$ subadditive, so the limit is also the infimum over $n$. Rains's converse gives $\Eppt(\rho) \leq R^\infty(\rho)$. Regularisation cannot in general be omitted: Wang and Duan exhibited two-qubit states with $R(\rho^{\otimes2}) < 2R(\rho)$~\cite[Theorem~1]{nonadditivity-Rains}.

Recall the measured relative entropy~\cite{Donald1986} and the measured Rains bound. A finite measurement channel $\MM$ is represented by a finite POVM $\pazocal{E} = (E_j)_j$ through $\MM(X) = \sumno_j\Tr\!\left[XE_j\right]\ketbraa{j}{j}$, where the output basis is indexed by the outcomes. Then
\bb
D^M(\rho\|\sigma) & \coloneqq \sup_{\MM}D(\MM(\rho)\|\MM(\sigma)), \qquad R^M(\rho) \coloneqq \inf_{\sigma\in\mathcal{R}(A:B)}D^M(\rho\|\sigma)\, ,
\label{measured_rains_definition}
\ee
where the supremum ranges over finite measurement channels. The following useful form follows from the variational and approximation results of Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi~\cite{Fang2025, FFF2025}.

\begin{lemma}\label{measured_rains_lemma}
For every bipartite state $\rho = \rho_{AB}$,
\bb
R^M(\rho) = \sup_{H>0:\,\left\|H^{\pt}\right\|_\infty \leq 1}\Tr\rho\log H\, .
\label{measured_rains_norm}
\ee
Moreover, denoting with $D$ the global dimension of $AB$, for all $n\in\N^+$ we have
\bb
0 \leq R(\rho^{\otimes n}) - R^M(\rho^{\otimes n}) \leq 2(D^2 + D)\log(n + D)\, .
\label{rains_measured_penalty}
\ee
In particular, $R^\infty(\rho) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n R^M(\rho^{\otimes n})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Combining~\cite[Lemma~19]{Fang2025} with the Rains support-function identity in~\cite[Eq.~(98)]{FFF2025} gives
\bb
R^M(\rho) & = \sup_{H>0:\,h_{\mathcal{R}}(H) \leq 1}\Tr\rho\log H,\qquad h_{\mathcal{R}}(H) \coloneqq \sup_{\sigma\in\mathcal{R}}\Tr\sigma H = \min_{K \geq H}\big\|K^{\pt}\big\|_\infty\, .
\label{rains_support_formula}
\ee
Thus every feasible $H$ admits $K \geq H$ with $\big\|K^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq 1$; operator monotonicity of $\log$ allows us to replace $H$ by $K$ without decreasing the objective. Conversely, $\big\|H^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq 1$ implies $h_{\mathcal{R}}(H) \leq 1$. This proves~\eqref{measured_rains_norm}. The estimate~\eqref{rains_measured_penalty} is~\cite[Lemma~16, Eq.~(24)]{FFF2025}, applied to $\{\rho^{\otimes n}\}$ and $\mathcal{R}(A^n:B^n)$; its hypotheses are verified for the Rains set in the same reference, Sec.~4.3.
\end{proof}

The following strong superadditivity of the regularised Rains bound was established by Ao, Philip and Streltsov~\cite[Lemma~1]{Ao2026}. We include a simple proof for completeness.

\begin{prop}[{\cite{Ao2026}}]\label{rains_strong_superadditivity_prop}
The regularised Rains bound is strongly superadditive:
\bb
R^\infty(\rho_{AA':BB'}) \geq R^\infty(\rho_{A:B}) + R^\infty(\rho_{A':B'})\, .
\label{rains_strong_superadditivity}
\ee
In particular, $R^\infty(\rho\otimes\sigma) = R^\infty(\rho) + R^\infty(\sigma)$.
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
Taking product witnesses in~\eqref{measured_rains_norm}, as in the proof of~\cite[Lemma~23 and Appendix~C]{Fang2025}, gives $R^M(\rho_{AA':BB'}) \geq R^M(\rho_{A:B}) + R^M(\rho_{A':B'})$: the logarithm of a tensor product is a sum of local logarithms, even when the input is correlated. Apply this to $\rho_{AA':BB'}^{\otimes n}$, divide by $n$, and use~\eqref{rains_measured_penalty}. Product inputs satisfy the reverse inequality by subadditivity of $R^\infty$.
\end{proof}

Proposition~\ref{rains_strong_superadditivity_prop} concerns arbitrary correlated inputs, rather than only tensor products. Full additivity was proved by Beigi, Rubboli and Tomamichel~\cite[Proposition~9]{BRT26}, using the asymptotic equipartition property of~\cite{Fang2025}. The measured-relative-entropy argument above makes the correlated-input extension immediate.

\section{A regularised formula for PPT distillable entanglement}
\label{achievability_sec}

We construct two functions of a state and a measurement, optimise over the measurement, and then regularise over copies. The first function retains the operator absolute values of the partially transposed effects, while the second replaces each of them by its operator norm. Although the two optimisations can differ on a single copy, their regularisations coincide and give the PPT distillable entanglement, as established in Theorem~\ref{regularised_formula_thm}.

\subsection{Definitions and elementary properties}

Let $\MM$ be a finite measurement channel represented by the POVM $\pazocal{E} = (E_j)_j$, with zero effects omitted. For a bipartite state $\rho$, define
\bb
\widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM) \coloneqq \sup_{y>0}\left\{\sumno_j\Tr[\rho E_j]\log y_j - \log\left\|\sumno_j y_j\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right\|_\infty\right\} .
\label{povm_f}
\ee
Here $y = (y_j)_j$ is a family of strictly positive real numbers, and $|H| \coloneqq (H^2)^{1/2}$ for a Hermitian operator $H$. The operators $E_j^{\pt}$ need not commute, and their absolute values need not sum to $\id$.

\begin{lemma}[(Dual representation)]\label{povm_dual_lemma}
For every state $\rho$ and finite measurement channel $\MM$ as above,
\bb
\widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM) = \min_\sigma \sum_{j:\ \Tr[\rho E_j]>0}\Tr[\rho E_j]\log\frac{\Tr[\rho E_j]}{\Tr\!\left[\sigma\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right]}\, ,
\label{povm_dual}
\ee
where the minimum is over normalised states, finite, and attained. Positive-probability terms with zero denominator have value $+\infty$, and zero-probability terms are zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We use the linearisation of the logarithmic penalty in~\cite[Lemma~1]{Berta2017}, followed by Sion's minimax theorem~\cite[p.~174]{Sion}. Optimising a common positive scale of $y$ in~\eqref{povm_f} gives
\bb
\widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM) &\eqt{(i)} \sup_{y>0}\min_\sigma\left\{\sumno_j\Tr[\rho E_j]\log y_j + \frac{1 - \sumno_j y_j\Tr\!\left[\sigma\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right]}{\ln2}\right\}\\
&\eqt{(ii)} \min_\sigma\sup_{y>0}\left\{\sumno_j\Tr[\rho E_j]\log y_j + \frac{1 - \sumno_j y_j\Tr\!\left[\sigma\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right]}{\ln2}\right\} .
\label{povm_sion}
\ee
For (i), the best scale makes $\big\|\sumno_j y_j\,\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\big\|_\infty = 1$, and the norm is the maximum expectation over states. For (ii), the state space is compact and convex, the positive orthant is convex, and the displayed objective is continuous, affine in $\sigma$ and concave in $y$. These are precisely the hypotheses of Sion's theorem; compactness of the positive orthant is not required. The inner supremum separates over $j$ and gives~\eqref{povm_dual}: when both traces are positive, its maximiser is $y_j = \Tr[\rho E_j]\big/\Tr\!\big[\sigma|E_j^{\pt}|\big]$; the remaining cases follow by taking $y_j \to 0^+$ or $y_j\to\infty$. The maximally mixed state gives positive denominators for every nonzero effect, so the minimum is finite; lower semicontinuity and compactness show that it is attained.
\end{proof}

Bounding each denominator in~\eqref{povm_dual} with $\Tr \sigma\big|E_j^{\pt}\big| \leq \big\|E_j^{\pt}\big\|_\infty$ gives the simpler function
\bb
\widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM) \geq \ell(\rho,\MM) \coloneqq \sum_{j:\ \Tr[\rho E_j]>0}\Tr[\rho E_j]\log\frac{\Tr[\rho E_j]}{\big\|E_j^{\pt}\big\|_\infty}\, .
\label{povm_g}
\ee
For a partition of the identity into orthogonal projections on $V\otimes V$, this is the score in~\cite[Theorem~6.4]{Rains2001}. The two scores can be negative. Equality in~\eqref{povm_g} holds exactly when the maximal-eigenvalue eigenspaces of all positive-probability $\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|$ have a nonzero common intersection, since a minimising state in~\eqref{povm_dual} must then attain every norm simultaneously.

For comparison with $L$ in~\eqref{L_definition}, we optimise over finite measurement channels and define the auxiliary functional
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) \coloneqq \sup_{\MM}\widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM)\, ,\qquad L(\rho) = \sup_{\MM}\ell(\rho,\MM)\, ,
\label{povm_regularised_scores}
\ee
together with its regularisation, alongside the previously defined $L^\infty$
\bb
\widetilde{L}^{\,\infty}(\rho) \coloneqq \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n \widetilde{L}\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, ,\qquad L^\infty(\rho) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n L\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, .
\label{FG_regularisations}
\ee
Both limits are well defined by Proposition~\ref{FG_properties_prop} below. No positive part is needed in these optimisations, since the trivial measurement gives $\widetilde{\ell} = \ell = 0$.

\begin{prop}[(Elementary properties of $\widetilde{L}$ and $L$)]\label{FG_properties_prop}
For finite-dimensional bipartite states, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The functions $\widetilde{L}$ and $L$ are convex and satisfy
\bb
0 \leq L(\rho) \leq \widetilde{L}(\rho) \leq \log\big\|\rho^{\pt}\big\|_1\, .
\label{fg_bounds}
\ee
In particular, they vanish on PPT states.
\item Both functions are strongly superadditive:
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho_{AA':BB'}) & \geq \widetilde{L}(\rho_{A:B}) + \widetilde{L}(\rho_{A':B'})\, ,\\
L(\rho_{AA':BB'}) & \geq L(\rho_{A:B}) + L(\rho_{A':B'})\, .
\label{fg_strong_superadditivity}
\ee
\item For every PPT channel $\Lambda$,
\bb
L\big(\Lambda(\rho)\big) \leq L(\rho)\, .
\label{g_data_processing}
\ee
\item If $0 \leq A \leq \id$, $0 \leq A^{\pt} \leq b\id$, and $0<b<a \coloneqq \Tr[\rho A] \leq 1$, then, for the binary measurement channel $\MM_A$ represented by $(A,\id-A)$,
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) \geq \widetilde{\ell}(\rho,\MM_A) \geq \Dbin(a\|b)\, .
\label{f_binary}
\ee
\item Let $d \coloneqq \min\{d_A,d_B\} \geq 2$, and write $-\nu_1,\ldots,-\nu_r$ for the strictly negative eigenvalues of $\rho^{\pt}$. With
\bb
N \coloneqq \sum_{i = 1}^r\nu_i = \frac{\big\|\rho^{\pt}\big\|_1 - 1}{2},\qquad s \coloneqq \left(\sumno_{i = 1}^r\nu_i^2\right)^{1/2}\, ,
\label{npt_spectral_parameters}
\ee
we have
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) &\geq \max\left\{\begin{gathered}\Dbin\!\left(\frac{1 + s}{1 + \sqrt{\frac{d - 1}{2d}}}\,\middle\|\,\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{\frac{d - 1}{2d}}}\right),\\
\Dbin\!\left(\frac{d + 1 + 2N}{2d}\,\middle\|\,\frac{d + 1}{2d}\right)\end{gathered}\right\} .
\label{npt}
\ee
If $N > 0$ and $k \coloneqq \min\{\sqrt r,(d + 1)/2\}$, this further implies
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) \geq 1 - h_2\!\left(\frac12 + \frac{N}{2k}\right) \geq 1 - h_2\!\left(\frac12 + \frac{N}{d + 1}\right)\, .
\label{npt_rank}
\ee
Both terms in~\eqref{npt} vanish when $N = 0$. If $d = 1$, the state is separable and $\widetilde{L}(\rho) = 0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{prop}
\begin{proof}
For (i), a fixed-POVM $\widetilde{\ell}$ is a supremum of affine functions of $\rho$, while $\ell$ is convex because $p\log p$ is convex on $[0,1]$, with $0\log0 = 0$. Taking suprema over POVMs preserves convexity. The one-outcome POVM gives zero, and $\widetilde{\ell} \geq \ell$ follows from the dual representation in Lemma~\ref{povm_dual_lemma}.

For the upper bound, the trace inequality $\Tr[XY] \leq \Tr[|X||Y|]$ for Hermitian $X,Y$ follows by writing $X = X_+ - X_-$ and using $\pm Y \leq |Y|$. Consequently, for any positive weights, Jensen's inequality gives
\bb
\sum_j\Tr[\rho E_j]\log y_j & \leq \log\left(\sumno_j y_j\Tr[\rho E_j]\right)\\
& \leq \log\Tr\!\left[\big|\rho^{\pt}\big|\sumno_j y_j\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right]\\
& \leq \log\big\|\rho^{\pt}\big\|_1 + \log\left\|\sumno_j y_j\big|E_j^{\pt}\big|\right\|_\infty\, .
\label{fg_upper_bound}
\ee
Taking the two suprema proves~\eqref{fg_bounds}.

For (ii), let $\MM$ and $\pazocal{N}$ be represented by the POVMs $(E_i)_i$ and $(K_j)_j$ on $AB$ and $A'B'$, respectively. Their product POVM, with weights $y_i z_j$, has a logarithmic expectation equal to the sum of the two marginal logarithmic expectations. Its weighted absolute-operator sum is the tensor product of the two marginal sums, because
\bb
\big|(E_i\otimes K_j)^{\pt}\big| = \big|E_i^{\pt}\big|\otimes\big|K_j^{\pt}\big|\, .
\label{f_product_absolute_value}
\ee
Multiplicativity of the operator norm and optimisation prove the assertion for $\widetilde{L}$. For $L$, put $p_{ij} \coloneqq \Tr[\rho_{AA':BB'}(E_i\otimes K_j)]$, with marginals $p_i$ and $p'_j$. Direct expansion gives
\bb
\ell\big(\rho_{AA':BB'},\MM\otimes\pazocal{N}\big) = \ell(\rho_{A:B},\MM) + \ell(\rho_{A':B'},\pazocal{N}) + \sum_{i,j:\,p_{ij}>0}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p'_j}\, .
\label{g_product_expansion}
\ee
The last term is nonnegative, which proves the second assertion after optimisation. In particular, both functions are superadditive on tensor products and cannot increase when subsystems are discarded.

For (iii), the map $T \coloneqq \Gamma_{\rm out}\circ\Lambda\circ\Gamma_{\rm in}$ is a channel, so $T^\dag$ is unital and completely positive. For an output POVM $(E_j)_j$, its pullback $(\Lambda^\dag(E_j))_j$ has the same probabilities and satisfies
\bb
\big\|(\Lambda^\dag(E_j))^{\Gamma_{\rm in}}\big\|_\infty = \big\|T^\dag(E_j^{\Gamma_{\rm out}})\big\|_\infty \leq \big\|E_j^{\Gamma_{\rm out}}\big\|_\infty\, .
\label{g_pullback_norm}
\ee
Thus the pullback can only increase $\ell$, proving~\eqref{g_data_processing}. Zero pullback effects have zero probability and are omitted.

For (iv), both partial transposes are positive because $b<1$. If $a<1$, choose $y_1 = a/b$ and $y_0 = (1 - a)/(1 - b)$, so $y_1 > y_0 > 0$ and
\bb
\big\|y_1|A^{\pt}| + y_0|(\id-A)^{\pt}|\big\|_\infty & = \big\|y_0\id + (y_1 - y_0)A^{\pt}\big\|_\infty\\
& \leq by_1 + (1 - b)y_0 = 1\, .
\label{f_binary_norm}
\ee
Substitution in the definition of $\widetilde{\ell}$ gives~\eqref{f_binary}. If $a = 1$, take $y_1 = 1/b$ and $y_0\to 0^+$; the logarithmic expectation is $\log(1/b)$ and the norm has limit at most one, proving the same bound.

For (v), we may assume $N > 0$. Let $W \coloneqq (\rho^{\pt})_-$ and let $P$ be its support projector, so that $\Tr\big[\rho W^{\pt}\big] = -s^2$ and $\Tr\big[\rho P^{\pt}\big] = -N$. For a pure state $\psi = \ketbra{\psi}$ with Schmidt probabilities $(\lambda_i)_i$, the eigenvalues of $\psi^{\pt}$ are $\lambda_i$ and $\pm\sqrt{\lambda_i\lambda_j}$ for $i<j$. \bb

\label{npt_pure_state_bounds}
\ee

\bb
A &\coloneqq \frac{\id-W^{\pt}/s}{1 + q},\\
0 &\leq A \leq \id,\qquad 0 \leq A^{\pt} = \frac{\id-W/s}{1 + q} \leq \frac{\id}{1 + q},\\
\Tr[\rho A] &= \frac{1 + s}{1 + q}\, .
\label{npt_weighted_effect}
\ee

\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) \geq \Dbin\!\left(\frac{1 + s}{1 + q}\,\middle\|\,\frac{1}{1 + q}\right) .
\label{npt_weighted_threshold}
\ee
including the endpoint $s = q$.

Likewise, $\Tr\big[(\psi^{\pt})_\pm\big] = (\|\psi^{\pt}\|_1\pm 1)/2$ and $\|\psi^{\pt}\|_1 = (\sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i})^2 \leq d$ imply
\bb
-\frac{d - 1}{2}\id \leq P^{\pt} \leq \frac{d + 1}{2}\id\, .
\label{npt_projector_bounds}
\ee
In particular, $N \leq (d - 1)/2$. The effect
\bb
B &\coloneqq \frac{(d + 1)\id/2-P^{\pt}}{d},\\
0 &\leq B \leq \id,\qquad 0 \leq B^{\pt} = \frac{(d + 1)\id/2-P}{d} \leq \frac{d + 1}{2d}\id,\\
\Tr[\rho B] &= \frac{d + 1+2N}{2d}
\label{npt_projector_effect}
\ee
therefore satisfies item~(iv), which yields
\bb
\widetilde{L}(\rho) \geq \Dbin\!\left(\frac{d + 1+2N}{2d}\,\middle\|\,\frac{d + 1}{2d}\right) .
\label{npt_negativity_threshold}
\ee
including the endpoint $N = (d - 1)/2$.

For the comparison, the symmetric effects $(\id - W^{\pt}/s)/2$ and $(\id - 2P^{\pt}/(d + 1))/2$ are obtained from $A$ and $B$, respectively, by retaining an accepting outcome with probability $(1 + q)/2$ or $d/(d + 1)$. These stochastic acceptance maps act on the binary state probabilities, so data processing gives
\bb
\Dbin\!\left(\frac{1 + s}{1 + q}\,\middle\|\,\frac{1}{1 + q}\right) & \geq \Dbin\!\left(\frac{1 + s}{2}\,\middle\|\,\frac12\right) = 1 - h_2\!\left(\frac{1 + s}{2}\right),\\
\Dbin\!\left(\frac{d + 1+2N}{2d}\,\middle\|\,\frac{d + 1}{2d}\right) & \geq \Dbin\!\left(\frac12+\frac{N}{d + 1}\,\middle\|\,\frac12\right) = 1 - h_2\!\left(\frac12+\frac{N}{d + 1}\right) .
\label{f_spectral_thinning}
\ee
Since $s \geq N/\sqrt r$, this implies~\eqref{npt_rank}.\footnote{The rank estimate can also be obtained directly: partial transpose preserves the Hilbert--Schmidt norm, so $\big\|P^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq \big\|P^{\pt}\big\|_2 = \sqrt r$, while the preceding dimension estimates give $\big\|P^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq (d + 1)/2$. Thus $\big\|P^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq k$. Since $k \geq 1$ and $N \leq k$, the effect $(\id-P^{\pt}/k)/2$ has partial transpose between zero and $\id/2$, and acceptance $(1 + N/k)/2$; item~(iv) gives the first expression in~\eqref{npt_rank}.}
\end{proof}

Single-copy monotonicity of $\widetilde{L}$ under arbitrary PPT channels is not asserted here. In particular, the pullback proof for $L$ does not apply to $\widetilde{L}$, since absolute value does not obey $|T^\dag(X)| \leq T^\dag(|X|)$ for general unital completely positive maps. The regularisation of $\widetilde{L}$ is a PPT monotone by its operational identification with $\Eppt$ below.

For $H = \widetilde{L},L$, item~(ii) makes $H(\rho^{\otimes n})$ superadditive in $n$, while item~(i) gives $H(\rho^{\otimes n}) \leq n\log\big\|\rho^{\pt}\big\|_1$. Fekete's lemma therefore proves that the limits in~\eqref{FG_regularisations} exist and equal the corresponding suprema.

For $N > 0$, let $P$ again denote the strictly negative spectral projector of $\rho^{\pt}$. \bb

\label{npt_exact_projector}
\ee

\label{npt_exact_comparison}
\ee

Applied to the binary pair in~\eqref{npt_exact_projector}, the first produces the pair in~\eqref{npt_rank}, while the second produces the negativity-dependent pair in~\eqref{npt}. \subsection{Operational interpretation}

We now identify the regularised functions with the operational distillation rate. The achievability argument applies a fixed measurement repeatedly and selects its typical weighted outcomes; the reverse inequality follows by pulling back the Bell test of a distillation protocol.

\begin{manualthm}{\ref{regularised_formula_thm}}[(Regularised formula for the PPT distillable entanglement)]
For every finite-dimensional bipartite state, with $L$ defined by~\eqref{L_definition},
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\Eppt(\rho) = L^\infty(\rho) = \sup_{n\in\N^+}\frac1n\,L\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big)\, .
\end{aligned}
\tag{\ref{regularisation}}
\end{equation}
\end{manualthm}
\begin{proof}
Fix a block length $m$ and a measurement channel $\MM$ on $m$ copies, represented by the POVM $(E_x)_x$ and outputting a classical label $x$. Fix weights $(y_x)_x>0$ and put $h\coloneqq\sum_x\Tr\!\left[\rho^{\otimes m}E_x\right]\log y_x$. On $n$ independent blocks, accept the words $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ for which $\sum_{i=1}^n\log y_{x_i}\geq n(h-\delta)$, with any fixed $\delta>0$. By the law of large numbers, their summed effect $Q$ has acceptance tending to one as $n\to\infty$. Wordwise spectral calculus gives
\bb
-\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\big|E_{x_i}^{\pt}\big| \leq \bigotimes_{i=1}^n E_{x_i}^{\pt} \leq \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\big|E_{x_i}^{\pt}\big|\, .
\label{wordwise_spectral_bound}
\ee
Each accepted word has weight at least $2^{n(h - \delta)}$. Summing the corresponding positive bounds, and then adding the omitted positive words, yields
\bb
\big\|Q^{\pt}\big\|_\infty \leq 2^{-n(h - \delta)}\left\|\sumno_x y_x\big|E_x^{\pt}\big|\right\|_\infty^n\, .
\label{weighted_typical_bound}
\ee
Letting $\delta\to0^+$, equation~\eqref{channel} therefore achieves every positive rate below the objective in~\eqref{povm_f}, evaluated on $\rho^{\otimes m}$, divided by $m$. Discarding fewer than $m$ unused copies covers arbitrary total lengths. Optimising the fixed weights and measurement gives $\Eppt(\rho) \geq \widetilde{L}(\rho^{\otimes m})/m$, and hence $\Eppt(\rho) \geq \widetilde{L}^{\,\infty}(\rho) \geq L^\infty(\rho)$.

Conversely, pull back the Bell projection of an achieving protocol to $Q_n$. If its overlap is $1-\e_n$ and output rank is $d_n$, the measurement represented by $(Q_n,\id - Q_n)$ gives
\bb
L\big(\rho^{\otimes n}\big) \geq (1-\e_n)\log d_n - h_2(\e_n) - \e_n\log(1 + 1/d_n)\, .
\label{L_protocol_bound}
\ee
Indeed~\eqref{effect} and the triangle inequality bound the two partial-transpose norms by $1/d_n$ and $1 + 1/d_n$. Divide by $n$, let $\e_n\to0$, and take the supremum over achievable rates to obtain $L^\infty(\rho) \geq \Eppt(\rho)$. The superadditivity in Proposition~\ref{FG_properties_prop}(ii) and the linear bound in item~(i) give the limits and supremum formulae by Fekete's lemma.
\end{proof}

The same proof establishes the useful auxiliary identity
\bb
\widetilde{L}^{\,\infty}(\rho) = \Eppt(\rho)\, ,\qquad \widetilde{L}(\rho) \leq \Eppt(\rho)\, .
\label{auxiliary_regularisation}
\ee

Together with Proposition~\ref{FG_properties_prop}(v), Theorem~\ref{regularised_formula_thm} turns~\eqref{npt} into an explicit lower bound on $\Eppt(\rho)$ in terms of the spectrum of $\rho^{\pt}$, with the negativity relaxation in~\eqref{npt_rank}. In particular, every NPT state has a strictly positive rate. This makes quantitative the qualitative distillability theorem of Eggeling, Vollbrecht, Werner and Wolf~\cite[Theorem~1]{Eggeling2001}. The regularised functions are both monotone under PPT channels, either by their operational interpretation or by data processing for $L$ on every tensor power.

The regularised characterisation concerns vanishing-error rates. By retaining finite-block success bounds in the converse arguments, we also obtain exponential strong converses. We present the two converse constructions in separate subsections.

title: 2 Fast 2 Surgery: Fast surgery on QLDPC codes with $\tilde{O}(n(k + d))$ space overhead
abstract: We show that the fast surgery framework of Baspin-Berent-Cohen can be instantiated using at most $\tilde{O}(n(k + d))$ ancilla qubits, improving on the previously achievable $O(n\cdot k \cdot d)$ overhead. This result also establishes that fast surgery can be performed at a cost comparable to the $\tilde{O}(nk)$ overhead required for regular surgery. We build the surgery ancilla by first starting with a dense, but expanding system; and then applying expansion-preserving sparsification methods from gauging and code embeddings.
summary:
**TL;DR** This paper shows that the Baspin–Berent–Cohen fast (constant-time) surgery scheme for QLDPC codes can be run with only $\tilde{O}(n(k-\kappa+d))$ ancilla qubits when measuring a $\kappa$-dimensional subspace of logicals, improving the previous $\tilde{O}(nkd)$ and matching the $\tilde{O}(nk)$ cost of ordinary (slow) surgery up to the additive $nd$ term. The construction inverts the usual design logic: build a *dense* ancilla that manifestly expands, then sparsify it with gadgets proven to preserve expansion.

**The big picture** Logical operations on quantum error-correcting codes normally stall for a number of rounds proportional to the code distance; recent "fast surgery" schemes remove that delay but pay for it with a large block of helper qubits. The question is how cheaply such a helper system can be built. Here the author shows it can be built roughly as cheaply as for ordinary slow surgery, by starting from a helper system that has the needed robustness property but overly heavy parity checks, and then thinning those checks with transformations that provably do not destroy the robustness. This brings constant-time logical measurement into a space budget comparable to standard surgery, which matters for architectures where logical cycle time, not qubit count, is the bottleneck.

**Key contributions**
- Main theorem: a surgery ancilla complex that is 1-expanding relative to the projection onto the code, has the right homology image, preserves the cosystole, has $O(1)$-sparse $\partial_1$ and chain map, and has $\dim D_0 \le \tilde{O}(n(k-\kappa+d))$.
- A "dense expanding map" $\sigma = [\sigma_{\text{cocycles}};\sigma_{\text{boost}}]$ with only $O(k-\kappa + d\log n)$ rows, where $\sigma_{\text{cocycles}}$ kills unwanted logicals and $\sigma_{\text{boost}}$ is a random compression $R[H_{\text{logical}};\partial_1]$.
- A random-coding lemma: $t=O(d\log(em/d))$ random rows suffice to inflate all nonzero syndromes of weight $<d$ up to weight $\ge d$.
- The $d$-threshold property (stronger than relative systolic expansion) and proofs that Williamson's non-decongested gauging gadgets preserve it.
- A new *dual*-gauging (degree-reducing) gadget: replacing each high-degree qubit by an expander-graph vertex cluster (a generalized layer code), with explicit path-based correction map $\phi$ ensuring chain-map commutation.
- A slick cosystole-preservation argument: $\sigma\partial_2=0$ forces $(\ker\sigma)^\perp\subset Z^1(C)$, so added redundancies cannot shrink $\syst^1$.

**How it works** The ancilla is $\fib(\sigma)$ over a copy of the code itself (crucially $D_2=C_2$, which is what makes cosystole preservation work). Expansion is obtained by brute force: syndrome weights are boosted above $d$ by random coding. Then two sparsification passes — gauging (weight reduction via expander graphs attached to each row of $\sigma$) and dual gauging (degree reduction via expander data layers of size $\omega_\dagger+1$) — are composed into $\gamma^{\text{sparse}} = \gamma\circ\pi\circ\rho$, each step shown to preserve the threshold/expansion property, the homology isomorphism, and the cosystole.

**Why it matters** Relevant to anyone designing QLDPC architectures with low logical latency: it removes a factor of $d$ from the dominant space cost of the most general fast-surgery construction, and for constant-rate codes the result is optimal up to polylogs.

**Caveats** $\partial_2^{D^{\text{sparse}}}$ (the metachecks) is not sparse — the dual-gauging data layers force $\tilde\partial_2^A$ to act densely — so single-shot structure is lost; the author flags this as the main practical limitation and the key open problem. $\sigma_{\text{boost}}$ is existential (random matrix, no derandomization). Hidden constants from expander degrees and path choices are not tracked, and there are no numerics or threshold simulations. The near-optimality discussion leans on an $\Omega(k^2)$ lower bound whose citation is missing in the source.

title: A lower bound on the overhead of surgery on sparse stabiliser codes
abstract: We show that performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas requires $\tildeΩ(k^2)$ ancillary qubits in the worst case. As a result, for codes with large $k$, constant overhead ancillas can only realise a small fraction of possible measurements.
summary:
**TL;DR** A simple but sharp counting argument shows that any lattice-surgery scheme on a sparse stabiliser code, using sparse ancilla systems, must use at least Ω̃(k²/ω log n) ancilla qubits to be able to measure an arbitrary logical subspace. This nearly matches the Õ(tn) upper bound of recent parallel-surgery constructions, making it essentially tight (Ω̃(n²) vs Õ(n²)) for constant-rate codes.

**The big picture** Reading out logical information from a quantum error-correcting code is usually done by attaching an ancillary patch of qubits that fuses with the code — lattice surgery. Recent work has generalised this to arbitrary low-density-parity-check codes and to measuring many logical operators at once, raising hopes that readout could be made cheap even for high-rate codes. This paper shows a fundamental obstruction: if you demand the freedom to measure *any* chosen collection of logical degrees of freedom, the ancilla must grow roughly as the square of the number of encoded qubits, because there are simply far more possible measurement requests than there are sparse ancilla gadgets of a given size. The consequence is a space–time trade-off: cheap ancillas can only serve a tiny fraction of the possible measurements, so generic readout must be broken into many sequential rounds.

**Key contributions**
- A no-go theorem: for the set 𝓕 of subspaces a surgery scheme can measure, the ancilla size obeys N⋆ ≥ Ω(log|𝓕| / (ω log n)) — an "addressability vs. overhead" bound.
- Specialisation to all k/2-dimensional subspaces of the X-logical space gives N⋆ ≥ Ω(k²/(ω log n)).
- Demonstrates near-tightness of the Õ(tn) parallel-surgery construction of Cowtan et al. for constant-rate codes.
- Observes that near-linear-overhead surgery via "suitable subcodes" cannot be generically addressable when k ≫ √n, since such subcodes must be rare.

**How it works** Surgery is formalised as a symplectic embedding of an ancilla CSS chain complex D into the code's symplectic complex C, with a chain map g and defect map p; the measured subspace is [g](H₁(D)). Fixing ω-sparsity of ∂₁^D and g, the number of ω-sparse binary matrices of size s×t is at most (1+s)^{ωt} (binomial sum bound). Counting pairs (∂₁^D, g) over all dimension splittings d₀+d₁ ≤ N⋆ yields |𝓕| ≤ (1+N⋆)²((1+N⋆)(1+2n))^{ωN⋆}; combined with the Gaussian-binomial lower bound 2^{r(l−r)} = 2^{k²/4} on the number of k/2-dimensional subspaces, the result follows after eliminating the log N⋆ term.

**Why it matters** It sets a hard architectural limit for anyone designing logical readout for high-rate qLDPC codes: full addressability is not achievable at constant or linear ancilla overhead, and compilers must trade ancilla area against rounds of surgery.

**Caveats** The bound is worst-case over measurement sets, not a lower bound for any particular measurement; a scheme that only ever measures a restricted, structured family (small |𝓕|) escapes it entirely. It becomes vacuous for k ≲ √n. It constrains static ancilla gadgets per measurement; adaptive, reconfigurable, or multi-round protocols are not directly covered, and no matching lower bound on time is proved. Sparsity of both ∂₁^D and g is essential, and the bound degrades linearly in the weight ω and loses a log n factor relative to the known upper bound.
